extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and the scientific method
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of induction and logical relations
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of methods and principles for carrying out inductive reasoning and solving the inverse logical problem (inferring laws from observed combinations of properties). Presents definitions (perfect vs imperfect induction), exhaustive combinatorial methods, classification of logical law-types for two and three terms, and practical guidance for applying induction in science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove a proposition via its logical equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: We can always prove a proposition, if we find it more convenient, by proving its equivalent; to assert that all not-B's are not-A's is exactly the same as to assert that all A's are B's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proving 'all not-solids are not capable of double refraction' is equivalent to proving 'all double refracting substances are solids.' For questions of probability it is desirable, where possible, to prove both the original proposition and its equivalent to increase the area of observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide a class into exhaustive, mutually exclusive alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: When a class is divided into alternatives, show the required property for each alternative; substitution yields the property for the whole class (e.g., divide substances into magnetic and diamagnetic or solids/liquids/gases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If A = ABc + Abc and you can prove B = BD and C = CD then substitution gives A = AD, i.e., all substances in A possess D. Examples: magnetic vs diamagnetic → polarity; solids/liquids/gases → obedience to Carnot's law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for and classify exceptions (anomalous cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductions are often embarrassed by exceptions, real or apparent; such anomalous cases must be regarded and classified and expressed consistently in notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: diamonds combustible; very thin films of gold and silver transparent; some plants (fungi) not absorbing carbonic acid. Guidance: do not assume universality; record exceptions and incorporate them into classification or later treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat induction as the inverse problem: infer laws as exclusions of combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction consists in passing back from a series of combinations to the laws by which such combinations are governed; a law often means the exclusion from existence of certain combinations of terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent laws by which combinations are ruled out (using the 'logical alphabet'); deduce which law applies by determining which combinations are absent in observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use finite combinatorial enumeration and a consistency test
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite number of terms, the possible logical forms are finite; enumerate combinations of terms and negatives (e.g., for two terms there are four combinations) and test selections for consistency by ensuring each term has its negative somewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: two terms A,B give AB, Ab, aB, ab; there are 16 selections (2^4). Reject inconsistent selections (e.g., asserting both A=B and A=not-B destroys existence). Focus on columns of the combination table that meet the consistency test (each of A,a,B,b appears).

rubrics_metrics.name: Solve the inverse problem by exhaustive systematic variation (Sieve analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work out all combinations and try all plausible forms of proposition, varying by circular interchange of letters and by substituting negatives, marking off combinations accounted for; this exhaustive trial identifies distinct logical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to Sieve of Eratosthenes: enumerate all series, mark off those produced by a candidate law; repeated until all series accounted for. Example variations: AB = ABC varied by interchange/negative change to produce its logical varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorize all two-term relations into six canonical forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws governing combinations of two terms must be expressible either in a partial identity or a simple identity; the partial identity admits four logically distinct varieties and the simple identity two — six forms in all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A = AB (partial identity) and A = B (simple identity). Many apparent variants are contrapositives or equivalent and thus belong to one of these canonical forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify three-term relations into fifteen essential types
rubrics_metrics.description: For three terms there are 256 possible selections of the eight combinations; after removing inconsistent cases, there are fifteen conditions or series of conditions which may govern the combinations — fifteen essentially different kinds of arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The table (summarized) lists each type with the number of combinations contradicted and the number of distinct logical variations. Use this classification to recognize the logical form of three-term premises (e.g., Barbara is one of fifteen types).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify law type by the number of excluded combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: You may often deduce the form of the governing law by counting how many combinations are absent: e.g., seven combinations remaining (one contradicted) → eighth type; six remaining (two contradicted) → second, eleventh, or twelfth type, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic procedure: inspect observed combinations, count excluded ones, and consult the mapping to probable law-types; perform a limited number of trials (substitutions/negations) to determine the proper variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize practical limits: combinatorial explosion for four or more terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When the number of terms increases the number of possible combinations and selections grows explosively (four terms → 65,536 selections); exhaustive solution becomes impracticable beyond three or four terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer to analyze relations involving two or three terms directly; for four+ terms rely on alternative methods, partial enumeration, or domain-specific simplifications. Note published results (Clifford) give counts for four-term types but full tables are large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish perfect from imperfect induction and their roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect induction: all objects/events in the class have been examined; Imperfect induction: only some have been examined and hence involves uncertainty. Perfect induction is absolutely requisite both in performing imperfect induction and in treating large bodies of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imperfect induction is founded on perfect induction but requires different inferential treatment. First practical step in induction: accurately sum up the number of observed instances of the phenomenon. Examples: inferring gravity for distant stars from universality among known objects; using counts/frequencies to estimate probabilities (e.g., cryptogams cellular vs vascular).

rubrics_metrics.name: For probabilistic inferences, rely on frequencies and prove equivalents where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: When making probabilistic generalizations, estimate likelihoods from comparative numbers of known instances and, where practicable, prove both the original proposition and its logical equivalent to enlarge observational basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to estimate probability that a new cryptogam is cellular, use proportions among known cryptogams. For important probabilistic claims, seek corroboration by verifying equivalent formulations (increases area of observation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Express deductions and exceptions in consistent symbolic notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use consistent symbolic notation and substitution to express premises, alternatives, and derived results (e.g., substituting descriptions for alternatives in a disjunctive premise to obtain A = AX).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in text show transformations like substituting Bx, Cx, Px into A = B .|. C .|. P producing A = (B .|. C .|. Q)X and hence A = AX. Maintain consistent notation when representing classes, their negatives, and properties to avoid ambiguity.
